title: Sarika Tasnim
text: Hi, I’m Sarika, an engineer turned data enthusiast. I grew up in Bangladesh and studied Electrical and Computer Systems Engineering. Before MDS, I spent around three years working as an engineer and process analyst before deciding to go all in on data science. Now I’m here to build the technical depth I need to keep doing that work — and do it better.

title: Flipper Length by Species (R)
text:
Data: Palmer Penguins, Palmer Station Antarctica LTER.
In this post I compare flipper length across penguin species.

library(palmerpenguins)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

First, I remove rows with missing values.



Table 1: The original dataset


penguins_clean <- penguins |> na.omit()
head(penguins_clean)

1 Adelie  Torgersen           39.1          18.7               181        3750
2 Adelie  Torgersen           39.5          17.4               186        3800
3 Adelie  Torgersen           40.3          18                 195        3250
4 Adelie  Torgersen           36.7          19.3               193        3450
5 Adelie  Torgersen           39.3          20.6               190        3650
6 Adelie  Torgersen           38.9          17.8               181        3625
# ℹ 2 more variables: sex <fct>, year <int>




Next, I group the data by ‘species’ and summarise the mean, mininum and maximum flipper length for each species as well as the count for penguins in each species.Then sort the data in a descending order.

penguins_clean |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    mean_flipper = mean(flipper_length_mm),
    min_flipper = min(flipper_length_mm),
    max_flipper = max(flipper_length_mm),
    count = n()
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_flipper)) |>
  kable(digits = 1)

Finally, I compare flipper length across species with a boxplot.
This makes a boxplot with one box per species, showing how flipper length is spread out within each species. Each box is filled with a different colour by species, the axes are labelled “Species” and “Flipper length (mm)”, and the legend is hidden because the species names already appear on the x-axis.

ggplot(penguins_clean, aes(x = species, y = flipper_length_mm, fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(x = "Species", y = "Flipper length (mm)") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")







Figure 1: Flipper length by species.





Gentoo penguins have the longest flippers, while Adelie penguins have the shortest.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
Orientation day on campus.


MDS gave us a genuinely warm welcome. Over a few sessions, I got to meet my faculty and classmates, and the standout moment was easily the campus goose chase — a mix of fun and practicality, since it doubled as a way to explore campus (and I walked away with a free MDS backpack). The final day brought everything together with an alumni panel and a dinner that capped off three memorable days.
Jumping into actual lectures after four years away felt strange at first — everything was new again, and the sudden wave of labs and assignments made the week feel a bit overwhelming. But as the days went on, I found my footing. By the time the week wrapped up, I’d worked through most of the deliverables, and what started as chaos had settled into something a lot more manageable.
Looking back, the nerves from week one have mostly faded into cautious confidence. I still have a lot to learn, but I’m starting to trust that I can keep up — and I’m genuinely excited for what’s next.

Next, I compare the average body mass of each species. This code groups the penguins by species, calculates the average body mass for each one, rounds it to one decimal place, and sorts them from heaviest to lightest. reset_index() turns species back into a regular column so the result displays as a proper table, and the last line shows that table on the page.

avg_mass = penguins.groupby("species")["body_mass_g"].mean().round(1).sort_values(ascending=False)
avg_mass = avg_mass.reset_index()

title: About
text: I grew up in Bangladesh and studied Electrical and Computer Systems Engineering at Monash University Malaysia. My first real exposure to data came at British American Tobacco Bangladesh, where I spent over two and a half years as an engineer working on industrial analytics — including projects that used real-time machine data to predict equipment failures before they happened. I later spent six months at Robi Axiata, which gave me a different lens on how data drives decisions outside of manufacturing, before I decided it was time to formalize what I’d been learning on the job.

text: I grew up in Bangladesh and studied Electrical and Computer Systems Engineering at Monash University Malaysia. My first real exposure to data came at British American Tobacco Bangladesh, where I spent over two and a half years as an engineer working on industrial analytics — including projects that used real-time machine data to predict equipment failures before they happened. I later spent six months at Robi Axiata, which gave me a different lens on how data drives decisions outside of manufacturing, before I decided it was time to formalize what I’d been learning on the job.

title: About
text:
Why data science
Every role and experience I’ve had has circled back to the same realization: data holds the answers, but only if you know how to ask it the right questions. At BAT and Robi, I was constantly working with real data but often relying on intuition to fill the gaps I didn’t have the technical skills to close. MDS is how I’m closing them. I want to understand not just how to analyze data, but how organizations actually use it to transform the way they operate — and I want to be someone who can help drive that shift, not just watch it happen.

title: About
text:
Outside of data science
Outside of code and coursework, I’m usually planning my next trip. I love traveling and immersing myself in new cultures — it’s the same curiosity that drew me to data, just pointed somewhere more scenic. I also love a good concert or festival, and most weekends you’ll find me at one, or catching up with friends over good food.
